hierarchy.title: CHAPTER VII — POST-MARKET SURVEILLANCE, VIGILANCE AND MARKET SURVEILLANCE
Article 87 — Reporting of serious incidents and field safety corrective actions

exact_excerpts.text: 3. Manufacturers shall report any serious incident as referred to in point (a) of paragraph 1 immediately after they have established the causal relationship between that incident and their device or that such causal relationship is reasonably possible and not later than 15 days after they become aware of the incident.

4. Notwithstanding paragraph 3, in the event of a serious public health threat the report referred to in paragraph 1 shall be provided immediately, and not later than 2 days after the manufacturer becomes aware of that threat.

5. Notwithstanding paragraph 3, in the event of death or an unanticipated serious deterioration in a person's state of health the report shall be provided immediately after the manufacturer has established or as soon as it suspects a causal relationship between the device and the serious incident but not later than 10 days after the date on which the manufacturer becomes aware of the serious incident.

interpretation_limitations: The day counts are maximum limits and must be retained with the immediate-reporting and causal-relationship qualifications.

source.title: Q&A on repackaging & relabelling activities under Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and Regulation (EU) 2017/746

hierarchy.title: Do Article 16(3) and (4) of the MDR apply to 'legacy devices'?

exact_excerpts.text: ' Necessary in order to market' refers to conditions that should be met in order to market the device in that Member State. Whether a relabelling or repackaging activity is necessary, should be analysed on a case-by-case basis.
Examples of the abovementioned conditions may include (non-exhaustive list):

national language requirements for device information supplied by the manufacturer; the need to supply in a new package, a specific number of devices different from the number of devices supplied in the original packaging by the manufacturer, for reasons of: providing the healthcare system with pack sizes that are suitable for the needs of health institutions in that Member state; national practices authorising only a certain packaging size; health insurance rules making the reimbursement of medical expenses dependent on the size of the packaging; well-established medical prescription practices.

interpretation_limitations: The assessment is expressly case by case and the examples are non-exhaustive.

source.title: Questions and Answers on Custom-Made Devices and considerations on Adaptable medical devices and Patient-matched medical devices

exact_excerpts.text: Note 1: Adaptable medical devices (products which fall under (a) above) are mass-produced 2 medical devices which must be adapted, adjusted, assembled or shaped at the point of care, traditionally by a healthcare professional, in accordance with the manufacturer's validated instructions 3 to suit an individual patient's specific anatomo-physiologic features prior to use.

it is matched to a patient's anatomy within a specified design envelope using techniques such as scaling of the device based on anatomic references, or by using the full anatomic features from patient imaging; and
it is typically produced in a batch through a process that is capable of being validated and reproduced; and
it is designed and produced under the responsibility of a manufacturer even though the design may be developed in consultation with an authorized healthcare professional.

Different from a custom-made device, these devices are typically produced in batches or through mass production and do not require a written prescription by an authorised person (see Q6 for more information on written prescriptions).

According to MDR art. 16(1), a person (e.g. healthcare professional) who adapts, adjusts, assembles or shapes an adaptable medical device for a particular patient is not regarded as a manufacturer, as long as the adaptation, adjustment, assembly and shaping does not modify the device in such a way that compliance with the applicable requirements may be affected or changes the intended purpose. 4

cases.question: Under MDR Article 87(3)–(5), what are the maximum reporting deadlines for a serious incident generally, a serious public health threat, and death or an unanticipated serious deterioration in health?

required_answer_elements.text: For a serious incident generally, reporting is immediate after the causal relationship is established or is reasonably possible, and no later than 15 days after awareness.
For a serious public health threat, reporting is immediate and no later than 2 days after awareness.

For death or an unanticipated serious deterioration in health, reporting is immediate after the causal relationship is established or as soon as it is suspected, and no later than 10 days after awareness.

cases.question: According to the November 2024 EUDAMED gradual-roll-out Q&A, when do the VGL-module obligations become applicable, and which MDR provisions and subjects does its Q12 table list as concerned?

required_answer_elements.text: The source states a conditional trigger: six months after publication in the OJEU of the notice confirming VGL-module functionality; it does not establish a current calendar date.
Article 86(2) MDR maps to periodic safety update report.
Article 87 MDR maps to reporting of serious incidents, including periodic summary reports, and field safety corrective actions with field safety notice.
Article 88 MDR maps to trend reporting.

Article 89(5), (7), (9), and the third subparagraph of Article 89(8) MDR map to analysis of serious incidents and field safety corrective actions, exchange between national competent authorities, possible coordinated assessment and a coordinating authority, and manufacturer publication of the field safety notice.
A separate note says Article 90 MDR analysis of vigilance data will be implemented after the first mandatory VGL-module version is made available.

cases.question: According to MDCG 2021-3, how are custom-made, adaptable, and patient-matched devices distinguished, and what MDR market pathway applies to adaptable and patient-matched devices?

required_answer_elements.text: A custom-made device is made under an authorized person's written prescription with specific design characteristics under that person's responsibility for the sole use of a particular patient and their individual conditions and needs.
Mass-produced adaptable devices and devices mass-produced through industrial processes, potentially following a written prescription, are not custom-made devices.
An adaptable device is mass-produced and adapted, adjusted, assembled, or shaped at the point of care under the manufacturer's validated instructions to suit the patient's features.

A patient-matched device is matched within a specified design envelope, typically produced in a batch through a process capable of being validated and reproduced, and designed and produced under manufacturer responsibility; unlike a CMD it is typically batch- or mass-produced and does not require an authorized person's written prescription.
Adaptable and patient-matched devices are not CMDs and follow the standard MDR regulatory pathway for placing on the market.

Under MDR Article 16(1), a person who adapts, adjusts, assembles, or shapes an adaptable device for a particular patient is not regarded as a manufacturer as long as the activity does not modify the device in a way that may affect compliance with applicable requirements or change its intended purpose.
